OMITTED SPOUSE AND OMITTED CHILD (PRETERMITTED HEIR) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan T. Reyes · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Jordan T. Reyes, whose relationship to Pat Morgan is Surviving spouse, is reviewing this information sheet in connection with the estate of Pat Morgan. This sheet explains, on a general informational basis only, California's statutory protections for a spouse who married Pat Morgan, or a child born to or adopted by Pat Morgan, after Pat Morgan signed a will or created a revocable trust that later became irrevocable — protections that come into play when an estate plan is never updated to add that spouse or child. These are commonly called "omitted spouse" and "omitted (pretermitted) heir" statutes. This sheet states general facts about how those statutes work, including the exceptions that can defeat them. It does not identify whether any specific spouse or child actually qualifies as "omitted" under Pat Morgan's actual estate plan, and it does not advise Jordan T. Reyes or anyone else on what to do about any actual situation.

WHICH INSTRUMENTS THESE PROTECTIONS REACH
These omitted-spouse and omitted-child protections are not limited to a will. They apply to property passing by will through a decedent's estate, and separately to property passing under a trust — but only a trust that became irrevocable solely because the settlor died, not a trust that was already irrevocable for some other reason during the settlor's lifetime. A trust that remained revocable by Pat Morgan until death, then locked into place at death, is treated the same way a will is treated for this purpose.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "This part shall apply to property passing by will through a decedent’s estate or by a trust, as defined in Section 82, that becomes irrevocable only on the death of the settlor."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21600 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the instruments these protections reach (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21600.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute defining which instruments these omitted-heir protections reach — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. The statute cross-references the Probate Code's general definition of "trust" in Section 82; that separate definitional section is not independently quoted here, only the irrevocability distinction actually stated in Section 21600.

THE OMITTED SPOUSE'S DEFAULT SHARE
If Pat Morgan married someone after signing all of Pat Morgan's testamentary instruments — a term that includes both a will and a qualifying trust of the kind described above — and the estate plan was never updated to provide for that spouse, California law entitles the omitted spouse, unless one of the exceptions described in the next clause applies, to a default share of the estate: one-half of the community property belonging to Pat Morgan, one-half of the quasi-community property belonging to Pat Morgan, and a share of Pat Morgan's separate property equal in value to what the spouse would have received had Pat Morgan died with no will or trust at all — capped at one-half of the separate property in the estate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Except as provided in Section 21611, if a decedent fails to provide in a testamentary instrument for the decedent’s surviving spouse who married the decedent after the execution of all of the decedent’s testamentary instruments, the omitted spouse shall receive a share in the decedent’s estate, consisting of the following property in said estate: (a) The one-half of the community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 100. (b) The one-half of the quasi-community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 101. (c) A share of the separate property of the decedent equal in value to that which the spouse would have received if the decedent had died without having executed a testamentary instrument, but in no event is the share to be more than one-half the value of the separate property in the estate."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21610 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the omitted spouse's default share (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21610.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, automatic default — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. This share is calculated differently from the omitted child's share described further below: the spouse's default share draws on California's community-property framework (half of community and quasi-community property, plus a capped intestate-equivalent share of separate property), while the child's default share is simply the child's full intestate share, with no comparable cap.

WHEN THE OMITTED SPOUSE'S SHARE DOESN'T APPLY
The omitted spouse's default share does not apply if any of several things is established: that Pat Morgan's failure to provide for the spouse was intentional and that intention appears from the testamentary instruments; that Pat Morgan provided for the spouse through a transfer outside the estate plan, with intent that the transfer replace a provision in it; that the spouse signed a valid agreement waiving the right to share in the estate; or — a narrower anti-abuse rule — that the spouse was a paid "care custodian" who provided health or social services to Pat Morgan as a legally defined "dependent adult" (broadly, someone 65 or older unable to properly provide for their own physical needs or with certain cognitive deficits, or someone 18 or older with substantial difficulty managing finances or resisting fraud or undue influence because of a cognitive deficit), where the marriage began while that care was being provided or within 90 days after it ended, and Pat Morgan died less than six months after the marriage began — unless the spouse proves by clear and convincing evidence that the marriage was not the product of fraud or undue influence. A person who had an unpaid, personal relationship with the dependent adult predating certain statutory time thresholds is excluded from the definition of "care custodian" altogether.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The spouse shall not receive a share of the estate under Section 21610 if any of the following is established: (a) The decedent’s failure to provide for the spouse in the decedent’s testamentary instruments was intentional and that intention appears from the testamentary instruments. (b) The decedent provided for the spouse by transfer outside of the estate passing by the decedent’s testamentary instruments and the intention that the transfer be in lieu of a provision in said instruments is shown by statements of the decedent or from the amount of the transfer or by other evidence. (c) The spouse made a valid agreement waiving the right to share in the decedent’s estate. (d) (1) If both of the following apply: (A) The spouse was a care custodian, as that term is defined in Section 21362, of the decedent who was a dependent adult, as that term is defined in Section 21366, and the marriage commenced while the care custodian provided services to the decedent, or within 90 days after those services were last provided to the decedent. (B) The decedent died less than six months after the marriage commenced. (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), a spouse described by this subdivision shall be entitled to receive a share of the estate pursuant to Section 21610 if the spouse proves by clear and convincing evidence that the marriage between the spouse and the decedent was not the product of fraud or undue influence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21611 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, when the omitted-spouse share doesn't apply (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21611.)
  "“Care custodian” means a person who provides health or social services to a dependent adult, except that “care custodian” does not include a person who provided services without remuneration if the person had a personal relationship with the dependent adult (1) at least 90 days before providing those services, (2) at least six months before the dependent adult’s death, and (3) before the dependant adult was admitted to hospice care, if the dependent adult was admitted to hospice care."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21362 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the definition of "care custodian" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21362.)
  "“Dependent adult” means a person who, at the time of executing the instrument at issue under this part, was a person described in either of the following: (a) The person was 65 years of age or older and satisfied one or both of the following criteria: (1) The person was unable to provide properly for his or her personal needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter. (2) Due to one or more deficits in the mental functions listed in paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (a) of Section 811, the person had difficulty managing his or her own financial resources or resisting fraud or undue influence. (b) The person was 18 years of age or older and satisfied one or both of the following criteria: (1) The person was unable to provide properly for his or her personal needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter. (2) Due to one or more deficits in the mental functions listed in paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (a) of Section 811, the person had substantial difficulty managing his or her own financial resources or resisting fraud or undue influence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21366 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the definition of "dependent adult" used by the care-custodian carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21366.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific, real limits on the omitted spouse's default share — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. Two of these exceptions (an intentional omission shown in the instrument itself, and an outside transfer meant to replace a provision in it) have direct counterparts among the omitted-child exceptions described further below; the waiver-agreement exception and the care-custodian anti-abuse rule do not — the statute contains no equivalent "valid agreement" or care-custodian carve-out on the omitted-child side. The "care custodian" and "dependent adult" definitions quoted here are incorporated by cross-reference from a different part of the Probate Code (the presumption-of-fraud-or-undue-influence statutes, §§ 21360–21392) rather than defined within the omitted-spouse chapter itself.

THE OMITTED CHILD'S DEFAULT SHARE
A child of Pat Morgan who is born or adopted after Pat Morgan signed all of Pat Morgan's testamentary instruments, and who isn't provided for in them, is entitled by default — unless an exception described in the next clause applies — to a share of the estate equal in value to what that child would have received had Pat Morgan died with no will or qualifying trust at all. The same default share reaches a child who was already alive when the instruments were signed but was left out solely because Pat Morgan believed the child was dead or did not know the child had been born.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Except as provided in Section 21621, if a decedent fails to provide in a testamentary instrument for a child of decedent born or adopted after the execution of all of the decedent’s testamentary instruments, the omitted child shall receive a share in the decedent’s estate equal in value to that which the child would have received if the decedent had died without having executed any testamentary instrument."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21620 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the omitted after-born or after-adopted child's default share (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21620.)
  "If, at the time of the execution of all of decedent’s testamentary instruments effective at the time of decedent’s death, the decedent failed to provide for a living child solely because the decedent believed the child to be dead or was unaware of the birth of the child, the child shall receive a share in the estate equal in value to that which the child would have received if the decedent had died without having executed any testamentary instruments."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21622 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, a child the decedent believed dead or didn't know about (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21622.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, automatic protection for an after-born, after-adopted, or unknown-and-presumed-dead child — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. Unlike the omitted spouse's share described above, which is calculated using the community-property framework and capped at half the separate property, the omitted child's share is simply the child's full intestate share, with no comparable cap. A child already provided for elsewhere in the estate plan, or left out for a reason other than these two specific circumstances, is not an "omitted child" under this statute at all. The two citations below are separate, independently numbered sections of the same statutory chapter rather than independently authored sources.

WHEN THE OMITTED CHILD'S SHARE DOESN'T APPLY
The omitted child's default share does not apply if any of the following is established: that Pat Morgan's failure to provide for the child was intentional and that intention appears from the testamentary instruments; that Pat Morgan had one or more children and left substantially all of the estate to the omitted child's other parent; or that Pat Morgan provided for the child through a transfer outside the estate plan, with intent that the transfer replace a provision in it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "A child shall not receive a share of the estate under Section 21620 if any of the following is established: (a) The decedent’s failure to provide for the child in the decedent’s testamentary instruments was intentional and that intention appears from the testamentary instruments. (b) The decedent had one or more children and devised or otherwise directed the disposition of substantially all the estate to the other parent of the omitted child. (c) The decedent provided for the child by transfer outside of the estate passing by the decedent’s testamentary instruments and the intention that the transfer be in lieu of a provision in said instruments is shown by statements of the decedent or from the amount of the transfer or by other evidence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21621 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, when the omitted-child share doesn't apply (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21621.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific, real limits on the omitted child's default share — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. This section was amended effective January 1, 2025 (Stats. 2024, Ch. 80, Sec. 108.5); the quote below reflects that current, in-force text, independently re-verified rather than assumed unchanged. The "other parent" exception has no counterpart among the omitted-spouse exceptions described above, and the omitted-spouse chapter's care-custodian anti-abuse rule and waiver-agreement exception have no counterpart here.

HOW AN OMITTED SHARE IS ACTUALLY PAID
Once an omitted spouse's or omitted child's share is established, the law sets a specific order for satisfying it: the share is drawn first from any part of Pat Morgan's estate that isn't disposed of by the will or trust, and only if that isn't enough is the remainder taken proportionally from everyone who takes under Pat Morgan's testamentary instruments, based on the value each would otherwise receive, measured as of the date of death. If applying that proportional reduction would defeat the obvious intent behind some specific gift or provision, that gift or provision can be exempted from the reduction and a different apportionment, more consistent with the intent behind it, adopted instead.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), in satisfying a share provided by this chapter: (1) The share will first be taken from the decedent’s estate not disposed of by will or trust, if any. (2) If that is not sufficient, so much as may be necessary to satisfy the share shall be taken from all beneficiaries of decedent’s testamentary instruments in proportion to the value they may respectively receive. The proportion of each beneficiary’s share that may be taken pursuant to this subdivision shall be determined based on values as of the date of the decedent’s death. (b) If the obvious intention of the decedent in relation to some specific gift or devise or other provision of a testamentary instrument would be defeated by the application of subdivision (a), the specific devise or gift or provision of a testamentary instrument may be exempted from the apportionment under subdivision (a), and a different apportionment, consistent with the intention of the decedent, may be adopted."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21623 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, how an omitted share is satisfied (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21623.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how an omitted spouse's or omitted child's share is actually satisfied once established — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. This apportionment mechanism applies identically to both the omitted-spouse share (addressed in the chapter governing Sections 21610–21612) and the omitted-child share (addressed in the chapter governing Sections 21620–21623); the statute treats the two the same at this satisfaction stage, even though it treats them differently at the entitlement and exceptions stages described in the clauses above.

CERTIFICATION AND SIGNATURE
I, Jordan T. Reyes, certify that I have read this information sheet describing California's omitted-spouse and omitted-child (pretermitted heir) statutes, Probate Code §§ 21600, 21610–21611, and 21620–21623, that it states generally applicable California law rather than a conclusion about whether any specific spouse or child actually qualifies as "omitted" under Pat Morgan's estate plan, and that whether a particular person qualifies — and whether an exception applies — is a determination made from the specific facts and instruments involved, not something this information sheet determines, and not something it advises Jordan T. Reyes on.

Executed on September 3, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan T. Reyes: _________________________

Printed name: _________________________

Reyes, certify that I have read this information sheet describing California's omitted-spouse and omitted-child (pretermitted heir) statutes, Probate Code §§ 21600, 21610–21611, and 21620–21623, that it states generally applicable California law rather than a conclusion about whether any specific spouse or child actually qualifies as "omitted" under Pat Morgan's estate plan, and that whether a particular person qualifies — and whether an exception applies — is a determination made from the specific facts and instruments involved, not something this information sheet determines, and not something it advises Jordan T.
